prompt: What actually differs between a client-rendered and a server-rendered page of the same app?
hint: Both run the same script in the browser.

choices.text: Only the server-rendered one runs JavaScript
choices.why: Both run the same JavaScript in the browser; that is the common picture the section corrects.

choices.text: What the first response carries
choices.why: Right. The first response is either an empty container or the finished page.

choices.text: Which framework built it
choices.why: Every framework can do either. The planner does both with no framework at all.

choices.text: How large the stylesheet is after the build
choices.why: The stylesheet is the same file in both cases; the difference is in the HTML.

prompt: A page is drawn on your computer or in CI, once, before deploying. Which of the three answers is that?

choices.text: Server-side rendering
choices.why: Server-side rendering happens on each request, not before deploying.

choices.text: Hybrid rendering
choices.why: Hybrid is about who renders the pages after the first one, not about rendering ahead of time.

choices.text: Static generation, at build time
choices.why: Yes. The file is finished before anybody asks for it; lesson 3 is about it.

choices.text: Client-side rendering
choices.why: Client-side rendering draws the page in the visitor's browser, after it has arrived.

prompt: A page shows each signed-in person their own sessions. What does that rule out?
hint: Think about who else could be handed the same copy.

choices.text: One cached copy for all visitors
choices.why: Right. A page made for one person cannot be handed to the next.

choices.text: Rendering it on the server, as each request arrives
choices.why: The server can render a page per person on each request; that is what SSR is.

choices.text: Rendering it in the browser
choices.why: The browser can fetch that person's data and draw it; that is client rendering.

choices.text: Using JavaScript on it
choices.why: Nothing about personal data stops a page from running scripts.

prompt: Why does this course recommend installing on the computer you use rather than a virtual machine or an online one?

choices.text: The tools refuse to run inside a virtual machine or a browser tab
choices.why: They run there; the section says both other paths work.

choices.text: Timings are cleaner on an unshared machine
choices.why: Yes. The course measures speed, and shared processors make the numbers noisier.

choices.text: It is the only path that needs no Node
choices.why: Every path needs Node 22.

choices.text: Chromium cannot be downloaded online
choices.why: Nothing in the section says so; the reason is the measurements.

prompt: You open a new terminal after installing Node and `node --version` prints `v22.22.0`. The very first one printed `command not found`. Why?
hint: When does a shell decide its PATH?

choices.text: The tarball finished unpacking in the background
choices.why: `tar` had finished before the prompt came back.

choices.text: npm had to be installed separately first
choices.why: npm came in the same folder as node.

choices.text: Its PATH predates ~/.local/bin
choices.why: Right. Ubuntu's profile adds the folder only if it exists when the shell opens.

choices.text: The link only works after the computer has been restarted once
choices.why: A new terminal is enough; nothing needs a reboot.

prompt: `npm install --save-___` writes a version in package.json with no ^ or ~ in front of it.
hint: One word, the opposite of approximate.

prompt: `node node_modules/.bin/vite` stops with `SyntaxError: The requested module 'node:util' does not provide an export named 'styleText'`. What do you check first?
hint: The file is inside node_modules, and you never wrote it.

choices.text: `node --version`
choices.why: Yes. A missing built-in function in a file you never wrote is the sign of an older Node.

choices.text: The syntax of `src/main.ts`
choices.why: The error is in Vite's own bundler, before your code was read.

choices.text: Whether port 5173 is taken
choices.why: A taken port makes Vite move to the next one; it does not raise a SyntaxError.

choices.text: Whether Chromium was downloaded
choices.why: Vite does not use Chromium at all.

prompt: `npx vite` prints `Port 5173 is in use, trying another one...` and then `Local: http://localhost:5174/`. Where is your page?

choices.text: Nowhere: Vite gave up
choices.why: It did not give up; it took the next free port.

choices.text: At port 5173, served by both
choices.why: Two programs cannot listen on one port; the older server still holds 5173.

choices.text: At the address on the Local: line, 5174
choices.why: Right. 5173 is whatever was already running there.

choices.text: At port 3000, where server.ts listens
choices.why: server.ts is a different program and does not move ports.

prompt: You change Playwright from 1.63.0 to a later version in package.json and run `npm install`. The next launch says `Executable doesn't exist`. Why?

choices.text: npm deleted the old browser from the cache when it upgraded the package
choices.why: npm never touches ~/.cache/ms-playwright; the old build is still there.

choices.text: Each version drives its own Chromium build
choices.why: Yes. The install command has to run again for the new version's build.

choices.text: The system libraries are missing
choices.why: That error lists .so files; this one names a missing executable.

choices.text: TypeScript cannot read the new version's types
choices.why: Node strips the types without checking them; the error comes from the launch.

prompt: Why are `addSession` and `markDone` written to return a new plan instead of changing the one they were given?

choices.text: TypeScript forbids changing an argument
choices.why: It does not; the choice is the author's.

choices.text: To be testable and safe to call anywhere
choices.why: Right. A pure function needs no page and leaves nothing behind.

choices.text: Because a new object is faster to create than a changed one
choices.why: Copying costs a little more, if anything; speed is not the reason.

choices.text: So that the session is saved when the page reloads or the tab is closed
choices.why: Nothing is saved; a reload loses it. Lesson 10 is where the planner keeps things.

prompt: In the sample plan, how many minutes of study are planned for the week of 2026-10-19?
hint: Five of the six sessions fall in that week.

prompt: `mount` puts one click listener on the container, not one on each button. What does that buy?
hint: What happens to a button every time the page is drawn again?

choices.text: The buttons work even when JavaScript is switched off in the browser
choices.why: No listener of any kind works without JavaScript.

choices.text: Clicks reach the server faster
choices.why: A click on Mark done never reaches the server at all.

choices.text: Clicks keep working after every redraw
choices.why: Yes. The new buttons are inside the same container, whose listener is still there.

choices.text: Each button can be found by its position in the list
choices.why: A click finds its session by the id in data-done, never by position.

prompt: `curl -s http://localhost:4173/` returns the built planner. What is inside its `<main>`?

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. The script fills it later, and curl does not run scripts.

choices.text: The list of three courses
choices.why: That is what the browser draws after the script and the data have arrived.

choices.text: A copy of courses.json
choices.why: The data is a separate request the script makes.

choices.text: A message asking to enable JavaScript
choices.why: The planner has no <noscript>; the main is simply empty.

prompt: With JavaScript off, how many requests did Chromium make for the client-rendered home page?
hint: The HTML, and what it names that is not a script.

prompt: An admin screen is used all day by five signed-in people on office computers. Which cost of client rendering matters least to it?

choices.text: The slow first load
choices.why: Yes. It is paid once a day, and every click after it is handled in the browser.

choices.text: That the script must download before anything works
choices.why: That is the same first-load cost in other words, and it is the one that matters least here, not a different one.

choices.text: That the server must render every page
choices.why: A client-rendered app's server renders nothing; it only hands out files.

choices.text: That a search engine sees an empty page
choices.why: It matters even less, but it is not a cost of the screen's speed. A screen behind a sign-in is never searched.

prompt: Why can `server.ts` draw the same HTML the browser draws?

choices.text: It runs a hidden copy of Chromium
choices.why: No browser is involved; Node calls a function.

choices.text: It calls the same `page` function from `src/view.ts`
choices.why: Right. One function, called in two places, so the two results cannot disagree.

choices.text: Vite compiled the pages into HTML files during the build
choices.why: The build wrote one empty index.html; the server fills it on each request.

choices.text: It copies the HTML the browser sent back
choices.why: Browsers do not send pages to servers.

prompt: With JavaScript off, the server-rendered course page reads perfectly. What still does not work?
hint: Which parts of the page did mount make work?

choices.text: The links to other pages
choices.why: A link without JavaScript is an ordinary link, and the server answers it.

choices.text: The heading and the list of sessions
choices.why: Those are in the HTML the server sent; they need nothing.

choices.text: The stylesheet
choices.why: It was fetched and applied; it is one of the two requests.

choices.text: Mark done and Add session
choices.why: Yes. Both are handled by the script's listeners, and the server has no handler for the form.

prompt: You add a fourth course to `dist/courses.json` while `server.ts` is running, and do not restart it. What does the next request for `/` show?
hint: Look at where the server reads the plan.

choices.text: The three old courses, until the server restarts
choices.why: Only the shell is read once at start-up. The plan is read on every request.

choices.text: The four courses
choices.why: Right. The plan is read inside the request handler, so each request sees the file as it is then.

choices.text: An error, because the build is now out of date
choices.why: The JSON is read as data; nothing checks it against the build.

choices.text: An empty page until npm run build runs again
choices.why: The shell is unchanged and the data is read fresh; nothing empties the page.

prompt: In the hybrid planner, you open `/` and then click Git. Who draws the Git page?

choices.text: The server, because every address is a request
choices.why: The click is caught by mount; no request for a page goes out.

choices.text: The script in the browser
choices.why: Yes. pushState changes the address and the script draws from the plan it has.

choices.text: Both, and the browser keeps whichever arrives first
choices.why: Only one draws; the server is never asked.

choices.text: Neither: the browser shows a cached copy of the first page
choices.why: The Git page was never fetched, so there is no copy of it.

prompt: Which cost does hybrid rendering add that neither pure client nor pure server rendering has?

choices.text: A server that has to render the first page of every visit
choices.why: Pure server rendering has that too.

choices.text: A script the browser has to download
choices.why: Pure client rendering has that too.

choices.text: Two renderers that must agree
choices.why: Right. If the two disagree, the takeover changes what the person is looking at.

choices.text: No link previews
choices.why: The first page is server-rendered, so previews work.

prompt: What does the islands approach send as plain HTML with no script?

choices.text: The parts of the page that never change after they arrive
choices.why: Yes. JavaScript goes only to the parts that respond to something.

choices.text: The whole page, with the scripts added later on request
choices.why: Islands decide per part, not per request.

choices.text: Only the first page of a visit
choices.why: That is hybrid per navigation, a different arrangement.

choices.text: The forms, because forms work without JavaScript
choices.why: The planner's form is exactly the kind of part that gets a script.

prompt: What does Google's own documentation say about Googlebot and JavaScript?

choices.text: It never runs JavaScript, so a client-rendered page is never indexed at all, whatever it contains
choices.why: That is the folklore the section corrects.

choices.text: It runs JavaScript only for sites that pay for it
choices.why: Nothing in the documentation ties rendering to payment.

choices.text: It renders them in a later step, and still advises server rendering
choices.why: Right. Rendering is queued after the first fetch, and server rendering is still advised.

choices.text: It reads only the <meta> tags
choices.why: That is closer to a link-preview program than to a search engine.

prompt: A link to `/courses/git` of the client-rendered planner is pasted into a chat app. What will the preview say?
hint: The program that makes previews does not run scripts.

choices.text: The Git course's title and its sessions
choices.why: Those exist only after the script runs, which the preview program never does.

choices.text: What the static index.html says
choices.why: Yes. Every address of a client-rendered site sends the same first response.

choices.text: An error, because the page needs JavaScript
choices.why: The response is a valid page; it is just empty.

choices.text: The Git page, once Googlebot has rendered it and shared the result
choices.why: A chat app's program does not wait for Google or ask it.

prompt: Which reader does the choice of where to render NOT change, once the page has loaded?

choices.text: A link-preview program
choices.why: It reads the first response only, so the choice decides what it sees.

choices.text: A crawler that does not run scripts
choices.why: That reader sees an empty page or a full one depending on the choice.

choices.text: A screen reader
choices.why: Right. It reads the page after the scripts have run, whichever way it was rendered.

choices.text: A person on a slow train
choices.why: That person sees the first response for as long as the script takes.

prompt: With 300 ms added to every request, when did the client-rendered planner first paint?
Both slowed-down pages made the same four requests. Why did the server-rendered one paint about 300 ms sooner?

choices.text: Its server is faster than Vite's preview server
choices.why: Both answer in a couple of milliseconds; the difference is the waits.

choices.text: Its HTML is smaller
choices.why: It is larger: it carries the page.

choices.text: It skipped the request for the data
choices.why: It made it too, after painting.

choices.text: It painted without the script and the data
choices.why: Right. Three waits in a row against two: the HTML and its stylesheet were enough.

prompt: A page needs a 2-second database query before it can be rendered. When can client rendering show something sooner than server rendering?

choices.text: When it paints a frame before fetching
choices.why: Yes. The server-rendered page sends no byte until the query ends; a client-rendered shell can paint first.

choices.text: Never, because server rendering is faster in every case, slow query or not
choices.why: The section names exactly this case as the exception.

choices.text: When the visitor has turned JavaScript off
choices.why: Without JavaScript a client-rendered page shows nothing at all.

choices.text: When the query result is cached by the browser
choices.why: The query runs on the server; the browser has no copy of its result.

prompt: The planner gains accounts, and every page now shows one person's sessions. What happens to the build-time option?

choices.text: It is gone for every page
choices.why: Right. A file built once cannot hold each person's sessions.

choices.text: It still fits the home page
choices.why: The home page would show each person's weeks too.

choices.text: It becomes the best option, because it is fastest
choices.why: Speed does not help a page that is wrong for everybody but one person.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because the data is still courses.json
choices.why: The data would become per person, which is the whole change.

prompt: A school's public course catalogue changes once a week and arrives mostly from searches. Which is the reasonable choice?

choices.text: Client-side, because a weekly change is rare
choices.why: Visitors from searches need the content in the first response.

choices.text: Server-side on every request, for freshness
choices.why: It works, and pays a server per view for a page that changes once a week.

choices.text: Static generation, redone on each update
choices.why: Yes. The same for everybody, found by search, and rare to change.

choices.text: Client-side with a loading spinner
choices.why: A spinner is better than a white screen, and still shows a crawler nothing.

prompt: Put in order what happens before a client-rendered planner shows its list of courses.
items: It fetches the script the HTML names
The script runs and asks for /courses.json
The script draws the list into main

prompt: Match each way of rendering to what its first response carries.

pairs.right: An empty container and a script tag
The page, drawn for this request
The page, drawn before anybody asked

prompt: Making the script attach to HTML the server already drew, instead of drawing it again, is called ___.
